industrialisierung-imperialismus#section: Abroad, the great powers pursued imperialism. Great Britain ruled over a quarter of the earth, France built an empire in North Africa and Indochina, Russia expanded into Central Asia, and in 1898 the United States took the Philippines and Puerto Rico from Spain. Japan's victory over Russia in 1905 showed for the first time that an Asian power could defeat a European great power. Alliances such as the Dual Alliance of 1879 and the Entente cordiale of 1904 divided Europe into two camps that collided in 1914.

The population of Europe doubled in the 19th century, and millions of people moved from the countryside into the cities. Berlin grew from 170,000 inhabitants in 1800 to over two million in 1910. In the working-class districts, families shared one or two rooms with lodgers and night sleepers, water came from the courtyard, and sewage ran in open gutters. Cholera, which reached Europe from India in 1831, killed tens of thousands in such districts until sewer systems, waterworks and the discoveries of Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur pushed back the epidemics.

The world of work determined life. Around 1850 a factory worker worked twelve to fourteen hours on six days a week, and children from the age of eight or nine stood at the spinning machines because they were small enough to crawl under them. The first laws, such as the Prussian regulation of 1839 or the British Factory Act of 1833, restricted child labor but were hardly enforced. From famines such as the Irish one of 1845 and from the Silesian weavers' uprising of 1844, contemporaries learned that hardship could become political.

Toward the end of the century, living conditions improved noticeably. Wages rose, working hours fell to ten, and trade unions and social insurance offered protection in sickness and old age. Department stores, sports clubs, bicycles, cinemas and summer holidays at the seaside were part of a new leisure culture. Millions of Europeans, above all from Ireland, Italy, Germany and Eastern Europe, emigrated to America; between 1880 and 1914 alone, over 20 million people left the continent.

The natural sciences experienced their greatest flowering. Darwin's theory of evolution of 1859, the bacteriology of Koch and Pasteur, the electrodynamics of Faraday and Maxwell, the discovery of X-rays in 1895 and of radioactivity by Becquerel and the Curies changed the picture of nature and of humanity. Universities and research laboratories, above all the German ones, became engines of progress; the chemical industry developed synthetic dyes, fertilizers and medicines such as aspirin in 1899.

Religion and the churches came under pressure but remained powerful. In Germany, Bismarck fought the influence of the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf of the 1870s, and in France church and state were separated in 1905. At the same time missionary societies arose that went to Africa and Asia with the colonial powers, as did religious reform movements such as the Salvation Army, which took up the cause of the poor in the industrial cities. With the Red Cross and Bertha von Suttner's peace movement, new nondenominational forms of humanitarian commitment emerged.

Art and literature reflected the upheavals. The realism of Dickens, Zola and Fontane described life in factories and tenements, and the Impressionists around Monet painted railway stations, boulevards and the light of the big city. The mass press, lending libraries and compulsory schooling caused the number of readers to explode. The world's fairs from London in 1851 to Paris in 1900 with the Eiffel Tower of 1889 staged technology and colonies as a spectacle for millions of visitors.

The first industrialization rested on coal, iron and textiles. James Hargreaves's spinning jenny from the 1760s and Edmund Cartwright's mechanical loom of 1785 multiplied the production of yarn and cloth, and the puddling process and later the Bessemer process of 1856 made steel cheap. The railway network in Germany grew from six kilometers in 1835 to over 60,000 kilometers in 1910. Canals, steamships and, from 1869, the Suez Canal connected the markets of the world.

From about 1870 the second Industrial Revolution began with electricity, chemistry and the internal combustion engine. Werner von Siemens developed the dynamo in 1866, Thomas Edison a usable light bulb in 1879 and the first power station in 1882, and Carl Benz the automobile in 1886. New large enterprises such as Krupp, Siemens, Bayer, Standard Oil and US Steel employed tens of thousands of workers and formed cartels and trusts. From 1866 the telegraph connected Europe and America permanently, and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone of 1876 followed.

The world economy became a single market. Grain from North America and Russia, wool from Australia, rubber from the Congo and cotton from India and Egypt flowed into the industrial countries, which in return exported machines, textiles and capital. The gold standard secured fixed exchange rates, and London was the financial center of the world. This interconnection brought prosperity, but also crises such as the crash of 1873, and it often rested on the exploitation of colonies and plantation workers.
erster-weltkrieg-zwischenkriegszeit#titl: First World War and Interwar Period
erster-weltkrieg-zwischenkriegszeit#summ: The First World War destroys the old order of Europe; revolutions, fragile peace treaties and the Great Depression shape the turbulent years up to 1939.
erster-weltkrieg-zwischenkriegszeit#over: In the summer of 1914, the assassination of the Austrian heir to the throne in Sarajevo set off a chain of alliance obligations and mobilizations. Within a few weeks the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire faced the Entente of France, Russia and Great Britain. The short war that had been expected congealed in the west into a war of position in which machine guns, artillery and poison gas killed hundreds of thousands without the front moving appreciably.

The war became the first total war in history: entire national economies were converted to armaments, women took over the work of men in factories, and the civilian population suffered from blockade and hunger. In 1917 the balance tipped: Russia plunged into revolution and withdrew from the war, while the United States entered on the side of the Entente. In November 1918 the Central Powers collapsed, Emperor William II abdicated, and the Armistice of Compiègne ended the fighting.

The Paris suburb treaties of 1919 and 1920 reordered Europe and the Middle East. The empires of the Habsburgs, Romanovs, Hohenzollerns and Ottomans had disappeared; in their place came new nation-states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Turkey. The Treaty of Versailles imposed war guilt, territorial cessions and high reparations on Germany, which many Germans felt to be a humiliation. The League of Nations was meant to prevent future wars, but remained weak without the United States and without means of power of its own.

In Russia the Bolsheviks under Lenin established the Soviet Union, the first communist state, after civil war and terror. In Italy, Mussolini came to power with the Fascists in 1922; in Germany the Weimar Republic foundered on inflation, political violence and the Great Depression until Hitler took power in 1933. The crisis of 1929 caused unemployment to explode worldwide and strengthened radical forces everywhere.

The 1930s were marked by rearmament and aggression. Japan occupied Manchuria, Italy attacked Ethiopia, and in the Spanish Civil War from 1936 to 1939 Germany and Italy tested their weapons at Franco's side while the democracies looked on. When Germany attacked Poland in September 1939, the next world war could no longer be prevented.
erster-weltkrieg-zwischenkriegszeit#cons: Around 17 million dead, devastated landscapes and a traumatized generation shaped Europe; the war is regarded as the primal catastrophe of the 20th century.
Four empires disappeared, and the map of Europe and the Middle East was redrawn; many border conflicts up to the present day go back to this.
With the Soviet Union, the first communist state came into being, and it determined world politics until 1991.
Defeat in the war, the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression created the conditions for the rise of fascism and National Socialism.
The League of Nations failed, but it provided the model for the United Nations after 1945.
erster-weltkrieg-zwischenkriegszeit#keyF: In September 1914 the Battle of the Marne halts the German advance; by the end of the year the western front from the North Sea to the Swiss border has congealed into trench warfare.
In 1915 the genocide of the Armenians begins in the Ottoman Empire, claiming an estimated one million victims by 1916; in the same year the Allied landing at Gallipoli fails.
On 9 November 1918 the republic is proclaimed in Berlin; on 12 November women in Germany receive the vote and go to the polls for the first time on 19 January 1919.
Between 1918 and 1920 the Spanish flu kills at least 20 to 50 million people worldwide, more than the war itself.
On 11 August 1919 the Weimar Constitution comes into force; in the same year Walter Gropius founds the Bauhaus in Weimar.
In 1923 Germany experiences the occupation of the Ruhr, hyperinflation and Hitler's putsch; the Rentenmark and the Locarno Treaties of 1925 usher in a brief phase of stability.

In 1930 Gandhi leads the Salt March against British rule in India, in 1934/35 Mao's Red Army saves itself in the Long March, and from 1936 to 1938 Stalin has hundreds of thousands murdered in the Great Purge.
erster-weltkrieg-zwischenkriegszeit#sect: During the war, power shifted in all states toward the military and the governments. In Germany, from 1916 onward the Supreme Army Command under Hindenburg and Ludendorff effectively governed, stripping the emperor of power, pushing through unrestricted submarine warfare and, in the autumn of 1918, shifting responsibility for the armistice onto the parties of the Reichstag. The political truce between the parties proclaimed at the start of the war broke apart in 1917 over the question of war aims, when the Reichstag passed a peace resolution without annexations. In France and Great Britain too, determined wartime premiers took the helm in Clemenceau and Lloyd George, the press was censored, and opponents of the war were persecuted.

With proportional representation, referendums and a directly elected Reich president, the Weimar Republic created one of the most modern constitutions of its time, yet Article 48 allowed the president to govern past parliament by emergency decree. The republic was fought from the right and from the left: the Kapp Putsch of 1920 failed only because of the workers' general strike, and the political murders of Matthias Erzberger in 1921 and Walther Rathenau in 1922 showed the readiness for violence of right-wing secret societies. From 1930 presidential cabinets governed by emergency decree, and the parties of the center lost ground to the National Socialists and the Communists.

Outside Germany, new movements shaped politics. In Italy, Mussolini forced his appointment as head of government with the March on Rome in 1922 and built up the first fascist state by 1926. In the Soviet Union, Stalin prevailed after Lenin's death against Trotsky, whom he expelled from the country in 1929, and established sole rule with a secret police and camps. The British Empire came under pressure: in Ireland the Easter Rising of 1916 led by way of a war of independence to the Irish Free State of 1922, and in India the Amritsar massacre of 1919 turned Gandhi's movement of nonviolence into a mass movement.

The war changed the life of the civilian population profoundly. Millions of women worked in munitions factories, as streetcar conductors, in offices and military hospitals, and kept agriculture running; in Germany the number of women workers in the armaments industry rose to over two million. In the turnip winter of 1916/17, the British naval blockade led to hunger in German cities, from whose effects hundreds of thousands died. At the front, by contrast, the Christmas truce of 1914, when German and British soldiers in Flanders sang together, exchanged gifts and played football, showed how alien the hatred of propaganda could be to ordinary soldiers; in the following years the army commands strictly forbade such fraternization.

After the war, in Germany alone there lived around 2.7 million war-disabled, along with hundreds of thousands of widows and orphans whose support burdened state budgets. Women's suffrage was introduced in many countries in recognition of their wartime contribution: in 1918 in Germany, Austria and, with restrictions, in Great Britain, in 1920 in the United States, and in 1934 in Turkey; France followed only in 1944. In the cities arose the image of the New Woman with bobbed hair, short skirt, her own income and a cigarette, which the illustrated magazines celebrated and conservatives found outrageous. For the majority of women, everyday life remained determined by housework, poorly paid employment and a shortage of housing.

The interwar period was also a time of refugees: Greeks and Turks were compulsorily exchanged in 1923, Russians fled from the Bolsheviks, and Armenians from persecution. For the stateless, the League of Nations created the Nansen passport in 1922. In the United States, Prohibition banned alcohol from 1920 to 1933 and allowed smuggling and organized crime to flourish, while hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the South to the industrial cities of the North in the Great Migration. From 1930 the Great Depression brought mass unemployment, soup kitchens and shantytowns from Berlin to Chicago.

Art responded to the war with rupture and provocation. In 1916 émigrés in Zurich founded Dadaism, which with sound poems and collages mocked the reason of a world that sent millions to their deaths. Expressionists such as Otto Dix and George Grosz depicted mutilated soldiers and war profiteers, Käthe Kollwitz gave form to the suffering of mothers, and Erich Maria Remarque's novel All Quiet on the Western Front became a worldwide success in 1929. The Bauhaus combined art and craft into a functional design that shapes architecture and design to this day.

The Golden Twenties made Berlin, Paris and New York centers of a new mass culture. Jazz from the United States conquered the dance halls, radio began broadcasting in Germany in 1923, and in 1927 cinema moved from the silent film to the sound film. Films such as Fritz Lang's Metropolis, variety shows and revues, boxing matches and six-day races drew millions. At the same time conservatives and the churches resisted the big-city culture they regarded as immoral, and the National Socialists disparaged modern art as degenerate.

In science, the picture of the world was measured anew. In 1919 a British solar eclipse expedition confirmed Einstein's general theory of relativity and made him world-famous overnight; a few years later Heisenberg, Schrödinger and Bohr founded quantum mechanics. In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, and in 1922 Howard Carter opened the tomb of Tutankhamun. Religions came under pressure: the Soviet Union persecuted the Orthodox Church, Turkey abolished the caliphate, and in Mexico the conflict with the church led to the Cristero Rebellion.

The First World War was the first industrial war, in which the factory helped decide the outcome. The Hindenburg Program of 1916 subordinated German industry to the needs of armaments, and the Auxiliary Service Law obliged all men between 17 and 60 to work. Because the blockade cut off raw materials, substitute materials arose from paper clothing to war bread, and the Haber-Bosch process supplied nitrogen for explosives and fertilizer. New weapons shaped the battlefields: poison gas, which the German army first used on a large scale at Ypres in April 1915, aircraft, submarines and the tank, which the British first sent into battle on the Somme in September 1916.

The costs of the war had heaped debt on all states, and on Germany reparations as well. In 1923 inflation destroyed the savings and pensions of the German middle class; only the Dawes Plan of 1924 with American loans and the Young Plan of 1929 created a viable system of payments. Rationalization on the American model with the assembly line, time studies and large corporations such as IG Farben increased production, and mass products such as the radio, the refrigerator and the car changed the everyday life of the more prosperous. Charles Lindbergh's solo flight across the Atlantic in 1927 and the airships of the Zeppelin works announced the age of air travel.

With the first Five-Year Plan of 1928, the Soviet Union took a different path: within a few years the state built up heavy industry and power stations, forced the peasants into collective farms and caused famines in Ukraine and Kazakhstan in 1932/33 with millions of dead. The Great Depression ended the West's brief upswing: banks collapsed in Austria and Germany as well in 1931, countries sealed themselves off with tariffs, and world trade shrank dramatically. From 1933 the United States responded with the New Deal, and Germany under Hitler with job creation and rearmament.
zweiter-weltkrieg#title: Second World War and the Holocaust
zweiter-weltkrieg#summary: The National Socialist dictatorship leads Germany into the greatest war in history and murders six million Jews in the Holocaust; in 1945 war and terror end with unconditional surrender.
zweiter-weltkrieg#overview.0: On 30 January 1933, Reich President Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor. Within a few months the National Socialists eliminated democracy with emergency decrees, the Enabling Act and terror: parties and trade unions were banned, opponents were locked up in concentration camps, and the press and culture were brought into line. The state rested on the leader principle, a racist ideology and the aim of conquering living space in the east.
zweiter-weltkrieg#overview.1: The persecution of the Jewish population began at once with boycotts and bans on practicing professions, became state doctrine in 1935 with the Nuremberg Laws and escalated in the November pogroms of 1938. In foreign policy Hitler broke the Treaty of Versailles step by step: rearmament, the occupation of the Rhineland, the annexation of Austria and the destruction of Czechoslovakia. The Western powers gave way in order to avoid a war. After the pact with Stalin, the Wehrmacht attacked Poland on 1 September 1939; Great Britain and France declared war on Germany.
zweiter-weltkrieg#overview.2: By 1941 Germany dominated almost all of Europe. The attack on the Soviet Union in June 1941 was waged as a war of annihilation in which millions of prisoners of war and civilians died. With the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor the United States entered the war, which now raged in Europe, North Africa, the Atlantic and the Pacific. Stalingrad in the winter of 1942/43 and the landing in Normandy in 1944 brought about the turning point.
zweiter-weltkrieg#overview.3: In the shadow of the war the National Socialists carried out the Holocaust: the systematic, state-organized genocide of around six million European Jews. After mass shootings by task forces behind the eastern front, the Wannsee Conference of 1942 coordinated the deportation of Jews from all over Europe to extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka and Sobibor, where they were murdered in gas chambers. Likewise killed were hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma, some 300,000 people with disabilities and mental illnesses, political opponents, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses and millions of Soviet prisoners of war and Polish civilians. Resistance such as that of the White Rose or the uprising in the Warsaw Ghetto remained the exception and was brutally crushed.
zweiter-weltkrieg#overview.4: In the spring of 1945 the Allies advanced into Germany from all sides and liberated the camps. Hitler took his own life in Berlin on 30 April; on 8 May the Wehrmacht surrendered unconditionally. In the Pacific, the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki forced Japan's surrender in August 1945. The war had cost about 60 to 70 million people their lives, most of them civilians.
zweiter-weltkrieg#consequences.0: The Holocaust became the benchmark for the crime of genocide; the Nuremberg Trials established the punishability of crimes against humanity and the idea of an international criminal justice.
zweiter-weltkrieg#consequences.1: The United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 arose as a direct answer to war and genocide.
zweiter-weltkrieg#consequences.2: Germany and Europe were divided, the Soviet Union and the United States rose to become superpowers, and the Cold War began.
zweiter-weltkrieg#consequences.3: Millions of people were expelled or fled; borders in Central and Eastern Europe were redrawn, and the European colonial powers lost their predominance.
zweiter-weltkrieg#consequences.4: The memory of the Nazi crimes shapes Germany's political culture to this day, along with the obligation to defend democracy and human dignity.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.0: After the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933, an emergency decree suspends basic rights; on 23 March 1933 the Enabling Act strips the Reichstag of power, and on 10 May the books of proscribed authors burn in German public squares.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.1: In December 1937, Japanese troops in Nanking murder tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of civilians and prisoners of war within a few weeks.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.2: The Munich Agreement of 30 September 1938 hands Hitler the Sudetenland; the Hitler-Stalin Pact of 23 August 1939 divides Eastern Europe in a secret additional protocol.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.3: In May and June 1940 the Wehrmacht defeats France in six weeks, and on 18 June de Gaulle calls for resistance from London; in the summer and autumn the Luftwaffe fails in the Battle of Britain.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.4: In 1942 Midway in the Pacific and El Alamein in North Africa turn the fortunes of war against Japan and Germany, even before Stalingrad falls.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.5: On 19 April 1943 the last inhabitants of the Warsaw Ghetto rise up against the SS; on 20 July 1944 Stauffenberg's attempt to assassinate Hitler fails.
zweiter-weltkrieg#keyFacts.6: In February 1945 Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin settle the postwar order at Yalta; from 20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946 the major war criminals stand before an international court at Nuremberg.
zweiter-weltkrieg#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
The National Socialist state was not an orderly system but a web of competing power apparatuses all vying for Hitler's favor: the party, the ministries, the SS under Heinrich Himmler with the Gestapo and the concentration camps, Göring's Four-Year Plan authority and Goebbels's propaganda ministry. The Führer often decided late and vaguely, and the subordination of all levels to his presumed will drove the radicalization forward. The judiciary became a tool of the regime: special courts and, from 1934, the People's Court handed down tens of thousands of death sentences, more than 2,600 under Roland Freisler alone. Plebiscites with over 90 percent approval, mass parades and the cult of the Führer replaced democracy with staged consent.

In the occupied countries Germany ruled in different ways: in Poland and the Soviet Union a governor general and Reich commissioners ruled with terror and plunder, while in Western Europe cooperation was sought with native governments such as the Vichy regime under Marshal Pétain, which handed over Jews and sent workers to Germany. Collaborators such as the Norwegian Vidkun Quisling gave treason their name. Japan too established a rule in East Asia that was advertised as the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere but in fact rested on exploitation, forced labor and massacres.

The Allies held their alliance together despite deep differences. In the Atlantic Charter of 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill formulated war aims such as self-determination and freedom from fear and want; at Casablanca in 1943 they demanded unconditional surrender; and at Tehran in 1943 and Yalta in 1945 they agreed with Stalin on the second front, the borders of Poland and the division of Germany into occupation zones. Resistance to Hitler came from many directions: from the carpenter Georg Elser, whose bomb missed Hitler by a few minutes in November 1939, from communist cells, the Red Orchestra, the Kreisau Circle around Helmuth James von Moltke, the officers of 20 July and the partisans in Yugoslavia, Poland, Italy and the Soviet Union.
zweiter-weltkrieg#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
The National Socialists promised a national community without class barriers and at the same time excluded all whom they declared alien or inferior: Jews, Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities, homosexuals, political opponents, Jehovah's Witnesses and so-called asocials. The Hitler Youth and the League of German Girls enrolled almost all young people, the labor service and the Wehrmacht the young men, and organizations such as Strength Through Joy offered travel and entertainment as a reward for conformity. Women were fixed in the role of mother with the Mother's Cross and marriage loans, but during the war they were deployed on a massive scale in armaments plants and as anti-aircraft and signals auxiliaries.

The war reached the civilian population with full force. The bombing war, which the German Luftwaffe had opened with attacks on Warsaw, Rotterdam and Coventry, struck German cities from 1942 onward: Hamburg in 1943 and Dresden in 1945 perished in firestorms, in all about half a million people in Germany died from air raids, and millions of children were sent to the countryside. Around 13 million foreign forced laborers and prisoners of war kept the German economy running; they lived in camps, were without rights and were often exposed to hunger and mistreatment. At the end of the war, twelve to fourteen million Germans fled from the eastern territories or were expelled, and hundreds of thousands died in the process.

In the Allied countries too the war changed everyday life. In Great Britain and the United States women replaced men in the factories, food was rationed, and children were evacuated from London. In 1942 the United States interned around 120,000 Americans of Japanese descent in camps, an injustice for which Congress apologized only in 1988. In the Soviet Union entire factories were relocated beyond the Urals, and the siege of Leningrad caused a million people to starve. In the occupied countries of Europe, everyday life meant hunger, raids, forced labor and the constant fear of arrest, while neighbors, pastors and entire villages such as Le Chambon-sur-Lignon in France hid the persecuted.
zweiter-weltkrieg#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
The National Socialists placed art and the media under state control through the Reich Chamber of Culture; anyone who was not a member was not allowed to work. Modern art was derided in the 1937 exhibition Degenerate Art, and thousands of works were removed from museums and sold or burned. The people's radio set brought Hitler's speeches into every home, Leni Riefenstahl's party rally films and the entertainment films of the Ufa distracted and enthralled, and the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin showed the world a peaceful, cosmopolitan Germany, while the African American sprinter Jesse Owens refuted the racial doctrine with four gold medals. Hundreds of thousands, among them Thomas Mann, Bertolt Brecht, Albert Einstein and most Jewish scholars and artists, went into exile.
